content: The term index case or primary case refers to the first identified patient in a population during an epidemiological investigation. This patient is not necessarily the first person to have been affected by the condition but is the first to bring attention to its existence. The index case may also be the first documented case of a condition or syndrome in medical literature, regardless of whether it is contagious. In some instances, the index case becomes a classic case in medical history, as seen with Phineas Gage. The index case can provide critical information about the source of a disease, its potential spread, and the reservoir that maintains the disease between outbreaks. It is the initial patient that signals the presence of an outbreak. However, earlier cases may later be identified and categorized as primary, secondary, tertiary, and so on. The term Patient Zero has been used to describe the index case in the context of the spread of HIV in North America. In genetics, the index case refers to the original patient (propositus or proband) whose condition prompts the investigation of other family members to identify potential genetic factors. The Case of Gaëtan Dugas (Patient Zero) During the early years of the AIDS epidemic, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) compiled a Patient Zero transmission scenario in 1984. The CDC identified Gaëtan Dugas, a flight attendant, as a carrier of the virus from Africa to the United States. He was believed to have spread the virus to other men he encountered in gay bathhouses. Journalist Randy Shilts later wrote about Dugas in his 1987 book And the Band Played On, based on findings by Dr. Darrow. Shilts portrayed Dugas as Patient Zero and a central figure in the spread of HIV among homosexual men in North America. Dugas, who was sexually active in multiple North American cities, was vilified for years as a mass spreader of HIV and was wrongly perceived as the original source of the epidemic. However, four years later, Dr. Darrow repudiated the study's methodology and criticized how Shilts had represented its conclusions. A 2007 study by Michael Worobey and Dr. Arthur Pitchenik, published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, used genetic analysis to suggest that HIV likely moved from Africa to Haiti and then entered the United States around 1969, possibly through a single immigrant. This study also highlighted that Robert Rayford, who died in St. Louis, Missouri, in 1969 from AIDS-related complications, was likely infected in 1966, indicating the presence of earlier carriers of HIV in North America. The term Patient Zero has since been adopted by the media to describe the index case in infectious disease outbreaks, computer virus outbreaks, and even as a metaphor for the origin of ideas or actions with widespread consequences. Other Notable Index Patients Mary Mallon (Typhoid Mary): Mary Mallon was an asymptomatic carrier of typhoid fever who infected 47 people while working as a cook. She was eventually quarantined to prevent further spread of the disease. Mabalo Lokela (Ebola Virus): The first recorded victim of the Ebola virus was Mabalo Lokela, a 44-year-old schoolteacher who died on September 8, 1976, 14 days after the onset of symptoms. Liu Jianlun (SARS): A 64-year-old doctor from Guangdong, Liu Jianlun, transmitted SARS during his stay at the Metropole Hotel in Hong Kong in 2003. 1854 Cholera Outbreak in London: A baby in the Lewis House at 40 Broad Street is considered the index patient of the 1854 cholera outbreak in London’s Soho neighborhood, as documented in Steven Johnson's book The Ghost Map. Édgar Enrique Hernández (2009 Swine Flu): Édgar Enrique Hernández, a young boy, is thought to be the index case of the 2009 swine flu outbreak. He recovered, and a bronze statue was erected in his honor. Maria Adela Gutierrez, who contracted the virus around the same time, became the first officially confirmed fatality.
